Environmental Enrichment for Early Stroke Rehabilitation: A Systematic Review
abstract: Stroke remains a leading cause of long-term disability, and the first 12 weeks after stroke represent a period of heightened neuroplasticity during which activity-dependent stimulation may support neurological recovery. Environmental enrichment (EE) has been proposed as a potentially low-cost strategy to increase meaningful physical, cognitive, and social engagement beyond scheduled rehabilitation sessions. However, evidence regarding its effectiveness in early stroke rehabilitation has remained limited. This systematic review aimed to identify, critically appraise, and synthesize comparative evidence on EE during early inpatient stroke rehabilitation, focusing on activity levels, safety, functional recovery, and psychological well-being, while evaluating methodological quality and risk of bias. Four databases—PubMed, ScienceDirect, Europe PMC, and Epistemonikos—were searched, yielding 492 records. Following screening, two nonrandomized controlled studies met the inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was appraised using Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) critical appraisal worksheets, risk of bias was assessed using the Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated qualitatively according to the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Both studies reported increased overall, physical, and social activity and reduced inactivity following EE interventions. Improvements appeared greater in acute stroke settings than in subacute rehabilitation, where limited fidelity to individually tailored enrichment protocols may have attenuated intervention effects. Neither study identified an increased risk of adverse events, and one reported fewer adverse events and a shorter hospital length of stay. Neither study demonstrated statistically significant improvements in functional outcomes or quality of life at three months. Overall risk of bias was rated serious in one study and moderate in the other, while certainty of evidence ranged from low to very low across the assessed outcomes. These findings suggested that EE may be a feasible and potentially low-cost adjunct to early inpatient stroke rehabilitation, with benefits for daily activity and engagement. However, the limited evidence did not establish its long-term effectiveness in improving functional recovery or reducing disability.

title: Hugo RAS versus da Vinci Xi for robot-assisted simple hysterectomy in endometrial cancer: a concurrent-period comparison of operative efficiency, cost structure, and the cost of early adoption
abstract: Abstract Assessing a newly introduced robotic platform is complicated by structural confounding between platform and calendar time, which makes device-specific performance hard to separate from early-adoption learning. We compared the Hugo robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) system with the da Vinci Xi in robot-assisted simple hysterectomy for endometrial cancer, confining the primary analysis to the period of concurrent use of the two platforms. This single-centre retrospective cohort included 219 patients with clinical stage I endometrial cancer operated between May 2018 and November 2025; procedures involving lymphadenectomy or sentinel lymph node biopsy were excluded at eligibility so that operative time remained comparable. The Hugo RAS was introduced on 4 December 2023, and the standardised mean difference (SMD) for operative month across the full period was 2.10; the primary analysis was therefore limited to 67 concurrent-period procedures (da Vinci Xi 37, Hugo RAS 30; SMD 0.66). Time outcomes were modelled by linear regression and cost outcomes by gamma regression with a log link, both with robust standard errors. In the concurrent period, the adjusted mean difference in total operative time was 16.3 min (95% confidence interval [CI] 6.0–26.6; p = 0.002), falling to 6.1 min (95% CI − 0.7 to 13.0; p = 0.080) when the first ten Hugo RAS procedures were excluded. Adjusted cost ratios favoured the Hugo RAS for consumables (0.808) and total operative cost (0.923), with no clear difference in reimbursement (1.013). The attenuation after excluding early cases points to an early-adoption contribution that cannot be separated from platform effects.

title: An IMU Dataset for Human Activity Recognition to Support Independent Living in Smart Homes (IMU-HAR-IL)
abstract: Abstract The majority of existing human activity recognition (HAR) datasets rely on wearable or object-mounted inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, yet they fall short in a critical dimension – they are not purposefully designed to capture the specific activities that serve as meaningful indicators of independent living among older adults. This document introduces HAR-IMU-IL, a dataset developed for HAR using IMU sensors within a smart home environment with a focus to support objective functional assessment of older adults’ independent living (IL). In particular, HAR-IMU-IL includes recordings of 50 participants performing 17 clinically relevant activities of daily living, spanning 4 functional domains essential for independent living: mobility, hygiene, nutrition and hydration, and medication intake. The dataset was collected using 30 IMU sensors, comprising both wearable and object-mounted devices integrated within a real-world residential setting. The dataset includes multi-sensor inertial data captured under realistic, unconstrained conditions, together with detailed annotations ensuring high temporal accuracy and consistency across sensors. A comprehensive data collection protocol was implemented to preserve ecological validity and enable reliable multi-sensor synchronisation. HAR-IMU-IL provides a large-scale, functionally grounded resource for advancing and benchmarking machine learning and artificial intelligence approaches for HAR in home settings. Its utility is further demonstrated by developing models capable of accurately recognising both activities and broader functional areas using wearable and object-mounted sensors. These capabilities highlight potential of the dataset to enable applications in continuous activity monitoring, functional health assessment, smart home automation, and assistive technologies that support independent living. By bridging the gap between raw motion sensing and semantic understanding of human activities, this work advances a foundational capability with broad implications for bioengineering systems design, robotic assistance, and clinical rehabilitation, where accurate, real-time recognition of purposeful human action is essential for responsive, adaptive, and personalised interventions.
